analysis.one_liner: Requires mortgage companies to try modifying loans before foreclosing on homeowners.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced mortgage lenders and servicers to work out affordable payment plans or loan modifications with struggling homeowners before foreclosing. It barred foreclosure if the company failed to follow the required steps, stopped second lien holders from blocking a modification of the first mortgage, capped late fees, banned forced arbitration as a condition of getting help, and gave borrowers a single point of contact and free access to their loan records. It also required regulators to rewrite servicer pay rules so companies are not paid more for foreclosing than for helping a borrower stay in the home.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners facing foreclosure on their primary residence. The bill would have required lenders to offer loan modifications, repayment plans, or forbearance before foreclosing, explain any denial, waive fees during the process, and barred second-lien holders from blocking a first-mortgage modification. Borrowers also got a toll-free line to an authorized representative, free account documentation on request, and doubled damages for servicer violations.

how_it_helps.text: Requires lenders to engage in loss mitigation—loan modification, repayment plans, forbearance—before any foreclosure, and voids any foreclosure sale conducted without it [S3].
Bars foreclosure while a borrower's written request for account records is pending, and gives borrowers free access to payment histories, the original note, and the identity of the loan's owner [S3].
Forbids requiring borrowers to waive their right to sue or agree to arbitration as a condition of receiving a loan modification, and caps late fees at 5% of the past-due payment [S3].
Requires second-lien holders to modify their loans in proportion to the first lien and, on underwater homes, to write down or release their liens, removing a major obstacle to keeping homes [S3].
Directs regulators to change how servicers are paid so the job does not reward foreclosure over loss mitigation, and raises civil penalties for violations [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders, loan servicers, and holders of second liens. They would bear the cost of mandatory loss mitigation, fee waivers and caps, free record-keeping and disclosure, and write-downs of junior liens on underwater homes, plus doubled damages for violations.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory write-downs of second liens and required modifications whenever a net-present-value test favors modification would impose real losses on lenders and junior lien investors, which could translate into costlier or scarcer mortgage credit for future borrowers [S3].
Voiding completed foreclosure sales for any past compliance failure could create legal uncertainty around home titles and generate litigation long after a sale [S3].
New servicing duties—single points of contact, onshore call handling, free documentation—add compliance costs that small servicers would feel more than large ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For homeowners in the middle of the foreclosure crisis, the protections were substantial and directly addressed the era's documented abuses: foreclosures processed without review, fees stacked on delinquent borrowers, and second liens blocking workout deals. The main costs fall on lenders, servicers, and junior lien investors, some of which could be passed to future borrowers through higher prices. As drafted it was an aggressive intervention, but its core mechanisms—mandatory loss mitigation before foreclosure—later became standard practice through regulation.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Financial Services Committee and its subcommittees for the rest of the two-year Congress and was never scheduled for a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on April 14, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1, S5].
On July 29, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Insurance, Housing and Community Opportunity and the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where it remained [S5].
It attracted one cosponsor and no further action; the committee never reported it, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and second-lien holders came out ahead: they avoided mandatory loss mitigation, fee caps, junior-lien write-downs, and expanded liability, and foreclosure and servicing practices continued as before under this bill.

for.name: Rep. Maxine Waters
for.role: U.S. Representative, CA-43; bill sponsor and senior member of the Financial Services Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor; as ranking member of the housing subcommittee she could not get the Republican majority to act on it.

for.name: 1 House Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only support it drew in the House.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in subcommittee until the Congress expired.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill and the Republican-controlled committee never moved it, though no vote was ever taken to confirm the split.

industries.note: Servicers would have been required to run loss mitigation before any foreclosure, take no fees during the process, provide free documentation, and accept pay rules designed to stop rewarding foreclosure. Servicer compensation that favored foreclosure over workouts was a core target of the bill.

Lenders faced mandatory loan modifications where the net-present-value test favored them, late fee caps, a ban on forced arbitration, and doubled damages up to $1 million for pattern violations. Their gain from the bill's death was the preservation of existing foreclosure and fee practices.

industries.industry: Second-lien and home equity loan holders
industries.note: The bill barred second liens from blocking a first-mortgage modification, required proportional write-downs, and forced principal reduction or lien release on underwater homes. Blocking workouts while collecting full payment was the business practice this targeted.

industries.industry: Foreclosure law firms and default servicing vendors
industries.note: Required fee waivers, free payoff statements, and documentation of every foreclosure would have reduced the volume of high-fee default work that these firms depend on.
